title: Counting Everything Loss to Gain Christ
summary: Paul warns the church against teachers who insist on circumcision and put confidence in the flesh. He lists his own impressive credentials as a Jew and a Pharisee, then says he counts them all as loss compared with knowing Christ and being found in him with a righteousness that comes from God through faith. He presses on toward the goal, urges the church to follow his example, and reminds them that their citizenship is in heaven, from where they await the Savior who will transform their bodies.
story: Chapter 2 held up the pattern of Christ, who did not cling to his status but emptied himself and was exalted, and then showed that pattern in Timothy and Epaphroditus. Chapter 3 shows it in Paul himself. He had more reason than anyone to boast of his religious standing, and he let it all go for Christ. The chapter begins as if the letter were closing (“Finally, my brothers”) and then turns sharply into a warning, which is one reason some scholars think Philippians joins more than one letter. Whatever its origin, the chapter carries the letter's great themes forward: the mind of Christ, joy in the Lord, suffering and resurrection, and life as citizens of heaven while living in a proud Roman colony.
historical:
The opponents in verse 2 are not identified by name, but the warning makes their main teaching clear: they insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to belong fully to God's people. Such teachers troubled Paul's churches in Galatia (Galatians 2 and 5), and Acts 15 records a council in Jerusalem, around AD 49, at which the apostles agreed that Gentile believers need not be circumcised. There is no sign that these teachers had yet reached Philippi; Paul may be warning the church in advance. Scholars debate whether the people of verses 18 and 19, whose god is their belly, are the same group (with belly referring to food laws and shame to circumcision) or a different group of believers who treated freedom as license.

Paul's own biography here matches what Acts and Galatians say. He was born into a Jewish family, circumcised as the law required, of the tribe of Benjamin (the tribe of Israel's first king, Saul, whose Hebrew name Paul also bore), a Pharisee, and a zealous persecutor of the church before he met the risen Christ on the Damascus road (Acts 9; 22; 26; Galatians 1:13-14).
cultural:
Dogs in the ancient Near East were mostly scavengers, not pets, and Jews sometimes used the word for Gentiles as unclean outsiders. Paul turns the insult around: those who demand circumcision are the real dogs. He also makes a sharp play on words. The Greek for circumcision is peritome, and he calls these teachers the katatome, the mutilation, the cutting that cuts off. The Pharisees, a Jewish renewal movement known for careful keeping of the law and its traditions, were among the most respected religious people of the time. To say one was faultless in legal righteousness meant a public record of careful observance, not a claim to sinlessness.

Philippi's citizens were proud of their status as a Roman colony whose people held Roman citizenship. Paul's word in verse 20, politeuma, refers to the commonwealth or citizenship to which a people belongs. Colonists thought of Rome as their true home and expected the emperor, often hailed as savior, to protect them. Paul says believers' true commonwealth is in heaven, and the Savior they await is the Lord Jesus Christ. The images of the race in verses 12 to 14 draw on athletic contests familiar across the Greek world, where runners strained toward a mark and a prize was awarded at the end.
literary: The chapter is an argument built around a personal example. After a brief call to rejoice (verse 1), Paul warns (verses 2 and 3), then gives his résumé in a carefully arranged list of seven items: four he was born with (circumcision, Israelite birth, the tribe of Benjamin, Hebrew descent) and three he achieved (Pharisee, zealous persecutor, faultless under the law). Then comes the reversal, framed in accounting language of gain and loss. Verses 7 to 11 echo the shape of the Christ hymn in chapter 2: as Christ did not count his equality with God something to cling to, Paul counts his privileges as loss; as Christ was obedient to death and was exalted, Paul wants to be conformed to his death and attain the resurrection. Verses 12 to 16 correct any impression that he has arrived, using the imagery of a race. Verses 17 to 21 contrast two ways of life, one ending in destruction, the other in transformation.

outline.t: Rejoice in the Lord, and beware of those who trust the flesh
Paul's reasons for confidence in the flesh
Counting all things loss to know Christ
Enemies of the cross and citizens of heaven

doctrines.note: Paul contrasts two kinds of righteousness: his own, based on the law, and the righteousness that comes from God and is received through faith (verse 9). Being right with God is a gift received by trusting Christ, not a status earned by pedigree or performance. This is the heart of what the Reformers called justification by faith.

Paul's hope is bodily resurrection. The Savior will transform our lowly bodies to be like his glorious body (verse 21). Christian hope is not escape from the body but its renewal, and it rests on the power by which Christ will subject all things to himself.

Paul wants to know not only the power of Christ's resurrection but also the fellowship of his sufferings (verse 10). Suffering for Christ is not a sign that something has gone wrong; it is part of being conformed to the one who suffered first.

words.note: Zemia, loss. A commercial term for damage or loss written on the debit side of an account. With its opposite, kerdos (gain), it turns the passage into a ledger. Paul has moved every former asset to the loss column, not because the law or his heritage were evil, but because compared with Christ they could not be counted as the ground of his standing with God.

Skubalon, rubbish. The word refers to refuse, scraps thrown out for dogs, or dung, and it is deliberately coarse. Paul chooses a word that shocks. The privileges he once prized most, placed beside the worth of knowing Christ, are fit for the garbage heap.

Politeuma, citizenship or commonwealth. The word names the state to which one belongs and whose laws one lives by. In a Roman colony, it would bring Rome to mind. Paul does not tell the Philippians to leave the world, but to live in Philippi as colonists of heaven, under the rule of the coming Lord.

christ: The chapter shows Christ as the one worth losing everything to gain. Knowing him surpasses every religious advantage (verse 8), being found in him is the only safe place to stand before God (verse 9), and sharing his sufferings and his resurrection is the shape of the Christian life (verses 10 and 11). Paul describes his whole life as a response to being grasped by Christ first: he presses on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of him (verse 12). The chapter ends with Christ as the coming Savior and Lord, who has power to subject all things to himself and to raise his people's bodies into the likeness of his own risen body. What the hymn of chapter 2 said of Christ's humiliation and exaltation, chapter 3 applies to those who belong to him.

hard.q: Does the righteousness in verse 9 come through our faith in Christ, or through Christ's own faithfulness?
hard.a: The Greek phrase in verse 9, pistis Christou, can be translated faith in Christ or the faith (or faithfulness) of Christ, and the same question arises in Romans 3 and Galatians 2. The traditional reading, reflected in the Berean Standard Bible, takes it as believers' faith directed toward Christ: righteousness is received by trusting him. A reading that has gained support in recent decades takes it as Christ's own faithfulness, his obedience to death, as the ground of salvation, with believers' faith mentioned in the next phrase, on the basis of faith. Defenders of the traditional reading note that Paul clearly speaks elsewhere of believing in Christ (Galatians 2:16), while defenders of the newer reading note that it avoids redundancy and matches the obedience of Christ in chapter 2. Both readings agree that righteousness comes from God, not from the law, and both place Christ at the center. The question is how Paul described it, not whether salvation is by grace.

questions: What credentials, achievements, or advantages do you tend to count as gain before God? What would it mean to move them to the loss column?
Paul wants to know both the power of Christ's resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings. Why do you think he refuses to separate them?
If your true citizenship is in heaven, how should that change the way you live in the place and nation where you are?
